claims.text: High-entropy-alloy multilayer coatings contain alternating chemically disordered layers and distinct interfaces.
Resistance to time-dependent plastic deformation is governed by synergy between atomic-scale solid-solution strengthening and periodic multilayer interfaces.
High configurational entropy produces chemical disorder that contributes to solid-solution strengthening.
Chemical disorder produces local lattice distortions within each layer.
Local lattice distortions impede dislocation motion.
Multilayer interfaces act as barriers to dislocation pile-up.
Multilayer interfaces inhibit shear-band propagation and formation.
The combined effects of chemical disorder and multilayer interfaces reduce the rate of plastic deformation over time.
Coatings with higher chemical disorder and optimized interlayer spacing will exhibit lower creep rates than homogeneous coatings and multilayers with suboptimal interfaces.
Coatings with higher chemical disorder and optimized interlayer spacing will show delayed onset of plastic deformation relative to the stated baselines.
The proposed mechanism should dominate when dislocation-based plasticity is prevalent.
At extreme temperatures or under diffusional-creep-dominated deformation, the benefits of multilayer architecture and chemical disorder may diminish.
The optimal interlayer spacing and quantitative contribution of chemical disorder are not presently specified.
A controlled series varying interlayer spacing and chemical complexity while holding overall coating thickness constant can test the proposed mechanism.
